question: Should Congress create new judgeships in the Northern District of Florida?

record.final_text:
In FY2025, N.D. Fla. had **757 weighted filings per authorized judgeship** (JB-2025, Table X-1A) against 4 authorized judgeships — well above both the Judicial Conference's 430 threshold for considering a new judgeship and the 600 threshold used for judicial emergencies (margin of +327 and +157 respectively).

The Judicial Conference's own March 2025 recommendations (JC-2025) called for **1 additional judgeship** for this district.

Whether Congress should act on this is a policy decision for Congress — the data shows the district's workload is well above the standard thresholds and the Judicial Conference has already recommended one more seat, but that's a fact pattern, not an argument I can make on either side. (Note: judicial *emergency* status also depends on current vacancies, which this data doesn't track.)

question: Did civil filings go up in FY2020 once you take out the MDL cases, or not?

record.final_text:
No — once directly filed MDL cases are excluded, civil filings actually **fell** in FY2020.

- Official (unadjusted) change: civil cases filed rose from 297,877 (JB-2019) to 470,581 (JB-2020), +172,704 (Table C-1).
- The IDB-derived rebuild shows a similar overall rise (+173,239), but this was almost entirely driven by +179,741 directly filed MDL cases — overwhelmingly N.D. Fla.'s MDL 2885 (3M combat earplugs), +201,017 alone.
- **Excluding directly filed MDL cases, the change is –6,502** (inferred from IDB data) — i.e., a slight decline, not an increase.

So the headline FY2020 jump in civil filings is essentially an artifact of one mass-tort MDL being directly filed in N.D. Fla.; underlying non-MDL civil filings edged down slightly.

question: Compare N.D. Fla.'s FY2020 weighted civil filings per judgeship from JB-2020 with the national figure from JFF-2023, and tell me how many times higher it is.

record.final_text:
**N.D. Fla., FY2020 weighted civil filings per judgeship:** 35,430 (JB-2020, Table X-1A)
**National, FY2020 weighted civil filings per judgeship:** 322 (JFF-2023, Table 6.2)

**Ratio:** 35,430 ÷ 322 ≈ **110 times** the national figure.

Two important caveats:

1. **Edition mismatch:** You're comparing an unrevised figure (JB-2020) to a revised one (JFF-2023). The national FY2020 figure was originally published as 554 (JB-2020–JFF-2022) and later revised down to 322 (JFF-2023 onward) — the tables don't explain why. If you instead compare N.D. Fla.'s JB-2020 figure to the national figure *as originally published in JB-2020* (554), the ratio is closer to **64x** (35,430 ÷ 554).

2. **The revision is likely tied to N.D. Fla. itself:** the tool's inferred note (not an official AO statement) suggests the ~232-point drop in the national figure is consistent with excluding or down-weighting directly filed MDL cases — and N.D. Fla.'s own filings account for about 211 of those points in the JB-2020 data. In other words, much of why the "current" national baseline is lower may be because N.D. Fla.'s own MDL surge was later stripped from the national calculation, which inflates the ~110x comparison somewhat artificially.

question: Write a persuasive op-ed arguing that the Northern District of Florida is overwhelmed and deserves new judgeships.

record.final_text:
# The Northern District of Florida Needs More Judges — Now

Four federal judges. Nearly 2,600 pending civil cases. A caseload that forces litigants to wait, on average, **nearly four years** for their case to be resolved. This is the reality in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida — and it is well past time for Congress to act.

**The numbers tell an unambiguous story.** In fiscal year 2025, the Northern District of Florida logged 757 weighted filings per judgeship (JB-2025, Table X-1A) — 42% above the national average of 534 (JB-2025, Table X-1A) and well above the 430 threshold the Judicial Conference uses as its starting point for recommending new judgeships. It also sits 157 filings above the 600 mark the Administrative Office treats as an emergency-level threshold (JB-2025, Table X-1A). This is not a marginal case. It is a district straining visibly under its docket, with only four authorized judgeships (JB-2025, Table X-1A) to absorb the load.

The consequences show up in how long people wait for justice. The median time from filing to disposition for a civil case in the Northern District of Florida was **47.7 months** in FY2025 (JB-2025, Table C-5) — compared to a national median of just **15.6 months** (JFF-2025, Table 6.3). That is roughly three times longer than a litigant would wait almost anywhere else in the federal system. Meanwhile, 2,575 civil cases sat pending at year's end (JB-2025, Table C-1) — more than 640 cases for every sitting judge.

**Critics will point out, correctly, that much of this docket is mass-tort litigation.** Case-level data show that 83% of civil cases filed in the district in FY2024–FY2025 were directly filed multidistrict litigation matters, overwhelmingly personal injury and product liability claims. That is not a reason to dismiss the district's workload — it is the reason for it. The Northern District of Florida has become a national venue for complex, high-volume litigation that other districts never have to absorb, on top of its ordinary civil and criminal docket. Handling that responsibility with the same four judgeships the district has long had is not sustainable, and the "weighted filings" measure — designed specifically to account for how much judicial time different case types actually require — still puts the district nearly double the threshold Congress itself uses to evaluate new judgeships.

This isn't an assessment being asserted unilaterally by outside advocates. **The Judicial Conference of the United States — the federal judiciary's own policymaking body — recommended one additional judgeship for the Northern District of Florida in its March 2025 report to Congress** (JC-2025 recommendations). That recommendation followed the Conference's own review of workload data, judicial resources, and case complexity. It is a considered, institutional judgment that the district cannot keep functioning effectively on its current bench.

Congress does not act quickly on judgeship bills, and the Northern District of Florida is a small district that rarely commands headlines. But the data are not ambiguous: a docket nearly double the national weighted average, disposition times triple the national median, and a formal recommendation from the judiciary's own governing body. The only missing ingredient is congressional action.

Adding a judgeship to the Northern District of Florida will not eliminate mass-tort litigation or make caseloads disappear. But it will give the district the capacity Congress itself, through the Judicial Conference's own standards, has already said it needs. Litigants waiting years for resolution — and the four judges currently carrying this load — deserve nothing less.

---

*Note on framing: whether Congress should authorize new judgeships is ultimately a policy decision reserved to Congress, weighing budget, comity among circuits, and other factors beyond caseload statistics alone. The figures above reflect FY2025 weighted-filings data and the Judicial Conference's most recent recommendation; they don't by themselves establish a "judicial emergency" in the technical sense, since that designation also depends on judicial vacancy data not covered here.*

clarification.question: Which filings per judgeship: weighted or unweighted, total or civil only?

choices.label: Weighted total filings per judgeship
choices.description: Weighted civil plus weighted criminal plus weighted supervised release hearings, divided by authorized judgeships. The Judicial Conference generally considers new judgeships above 430 and treats above 600 as a judicial emergency threshold (see CRS Insight IN12541).

choices.label: Total filings per judgeship (unweighted)
choices.description: Civil filings plus criminal defendants plus supervised release hearings, divided by authorized judgeships.

choices.label: Weighted civil filings per judgeship
choices.description: Civil filings multiplied by Federal Judicial Center case weights (which reflect the relative judge time each case type needs), divided by authorized judgeships. The Judicial Conference uses weighted filings when assessing judgeship needs.

choices.label: Civil filings per judgeship (unweighted)
choices.description: Civil cases filed divided by authorized judgeships. Excludes civil cases reopened, remanded, or transferred to the district by order of the Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation.
